translation:
It is worth understanding that in her previous birth she was Shurpanakha. It is not fitting that Manthara should be born as Kubja — even though Kubja was a hunchback, how could the ill-natured Manthara wish for Ram to become her own husband? Therefore Kubja could well be Shurpanakha, who, demoness though she was, had come to feel a true love for Ram.

Register No. 230, page 1517, writes: Who was this Kubja before? In the Ram incarnation, in Dashrath's palace, Kaikeyi had a maidservant named Manthara who was a hunchback, and so her name was Kubja. Before that she was a bird, and before that a gandharvi (celestial musician). In this incarnation her form was beautiful, but she was bent in three places — head, chest, and legs — so her name was Trivaka. Shri Krishna too is Tribhangi, standing bent at three points while he plays the flute.

Scholars who interpret this from a spiritual viewpoint say that Kubja means a mind bent in three places. What are those three places? Mind, speech, and body. According to Maharaj Jivanji's view, Shri Krishna is the one who, from being bent in three places (trivakta), becomes tribhangi and plays the flute. He is tribhangi. If we look at the deeper meaning of his standing bent at three places while playing the flute, it is this: Shri Krishna, breaking through the three gunas (qualities of nature — sattva, rajas, tamas) while he plays the flute, is the one beyond the three gunas. He who breaks through the three gunas while playing the flute is that same Shri Krishna who is beyond the three gunas. Because he is beyond the three gunas, the flute-charming Lord who is the true divine cowherd of Gokul is established as such — this is the conclusion Jivanji reached after discussing and deliberating with Gopaldas.

Register No. 251, page 276, writes: When Namdevji meditated and looked, he found that she (Janabai) had been Kubja in the Krishna incarnation. If we think along these lines, we could say that Harmabai, who was disabled from birth, could likewise have been Kubja in the Krishna incarnation, and just as Krishna healed her, Jivanji too removed Harmabai's disability and was united with her. We do not wish to make any claim of this kind, but it is shown in Jivanji's hagiography (parchari) that just as Maharaj Jivanji was Krishna's companion in the Krishna incarnation, Harmaba and the other fellow devotees were the gopas and gopis. That is fitting.

In the matter of guru and sadguru, Shurpanakha's incarnation as Kubja is consistent from the viewpoint of Samagam. Many speculations have been made about Kubja.

Shamal Haribhai's notebook no. 1, part 1, page 80 (Jagdish's no. 258):

The union of Kubja and Shri Krishna should be seen purely from a spiritual viewpoint. It is like the setting of the sun — each person interprets its meaning according to what suits them. For instance, one who performs the evening (sandhya) worship takes it as the sign for sandhya. A traveler on the road takes it as a signal to reach his destination quickly. A thief or a lustful person takes it as a signal to prepare for theft or seduction. Those who eat before sunset take it as a sign that eating is now forbidden — many such inferences (implications) can be drawn. In the same way, various meanings have been drawn about Kubja and Shri Krishna.

There is a Kubja-like disposition even in the ninefold devotion (navadha bhakti), because the goal is the attainment of Parabrahm. To atheists, devotion appears to be a sham. To those of other faiths, it appears to be a deliberate but faulty rite (kriya). To those driven by desire, it grants enjoyment according to their disposition, and for the desireless it purifies the inner being (antahkaran) and leads to the attainment of God — just as Kubja received the Lord's grace. Likewise, one who practices the devotion described in the scriptures also attains God. (Based on Bhagvat, Canto 10, Chapter 42, Shridhar's Ganesh edition, pages 88-89.)

Shurpa-karna — ears like a winnowing fan (shurpa): the winnowing fan separates the grain from the bad husk. The quality of the winnowing fan is that it separates Brahm from Maya.

Shurpanakha — one with nails like a winnowing fan: her nails perform the work of scraping and digging, like a hoe into the ground. Shurpanakha tried to win over Ram and Lakshman through her large nails. Maya presents her claws before Brahm, and, being unable to attain the love that resides in Brahm, she tries using her claws. But Maya's effort is not capable in that field of action, and so her nose and ears get cut off. Maya may be a portion of Brahm, but when Brahm wishes to remain within a limit (maryada), Maya's forceful attempt to merge with and attain it fails — this longing of hers was fulfilled in the Krishna incarnation, when she was wed as Kubja. When Brahm behaves not as one bound by limits but as Purna Purushottam (the complete Supreme Being), he cannot keep Maya separate from himself; if he did, Maya would be considered to have a separate existence of her own. Shurpanakha is consumed by desire (kama). Those consumed by desire regard even day as night — that is why they are counted among creatures of the night (nishachar).

_Diva pashyati no uluko, kako ratrau na pashyati; Apoorvah kopi kamandho, diva naktam na pashyati._
(The owl cannot see by day, the crow cannot see by night; but the one blinded by lust is unique indeed — he cannot see either by day or by night.)

The owl is blind by day, the crow by night, but one blinded by lust is blind both by day and by night. In broad daylight she went right up to Ram. Krishna is dark-complexioned, so for him it is easy to wed Kubja even in broad daylight. For one consumed with desire, night alone is considered suitable — she made even the night into a night six months long, and so plundered the gorasa (milk-curd) of the daytime.

Shamal Haribhai's notebook no. 4, part 2, page 194 (Jagdish's no. 265), writes:

It is mentioned in the Mathura Harivansh that Kubja, in her previous birth, was a king's daughter. Hearing Narad sing, she became enraptured with the Lord and desired to marry him. When the king spoke to Narad about a groom for his daughter, Narad said that the girl's own wish should be consulted. The girl said, "The one whose praises you constantly sing — him alone I wish to marry." Narad said that this could not happen. The girl said, "Even if it takes millions of births, I will marry none but him. Know this as certain." Seeing her unshakeable resolve, Narad showed her a way to attain the Lord. Seeing her austerities (tapa), the Lord's seat trembled, and a voice from the sky declared: "In your next birth you will become Kubja, and the one whose touch makes you beautiful will marry you." She was born in the house of Kansa's minister, and Kansa gave her the task of bringing sandalwood paste. The Lord says, "In whatever form one worships me, in that same form I meet them" — and it was owing to her own devotion that he had to meet her in this way. According to another version of the story, it is found elsewhere that Kubja was a partial form (amsha) of Satyabhama — she was the Earth, who had become bent under the weight of wicked kings. The Lord, with natural ease, straightened her and indicated by gesture that the Earth's burden was now about to be lifted. To think anything else about Kubja is ignorance. (Kalyan, page 785.)

Bhagvat, Canto 10, Chapter 44, verse 15, says:

_Kamam krodham bhayam sneham aikyam sauhadam eva cha; nityam harau vidadhato, yaanti tanmayataam hi te._ ||15||
(Those who constantly direct desire, anger, fear, affection, unity, or friendship toward Hari — they verily attain absorption in Him.)

Those who direct toward the Lord — in whatever way — desire, anger, fear, affection, unity, and the bond of fellowship, certainly become absorbed in the Lord.

Bhagvat, Canto 7, Chapter 1, verse 25, says:

_Tasmadvai ranushadhena, nivairan bhavena va; snehat kamena va yunjyat, kathanchin nekshate prithak._ ||25||

Canto 7, Chapter 1: "Oh! How did Shishupal attain a state that even good devotees do not attain?" When King Yudhishthir asked Narad this, Narad answered that God does not become disturbed by anyone's slander and the like. Therefore, through any of these five means — enmity, devotion, fear, affection, and desire — one should fix one's mind on God.

_Kamat dveshad abhayat, sneha-dyatha bhaktatyoshware manah; aavesya tadagham hitva, bahavastadgatim gataah._ ||24||
_Gopyah kamad bhayat kanso, dveshacyaidyadayo nripah; sambandhad vrishnayah sneha-dhuyam bhaktya vayam vibho._ ||30||

Just as the mind is fixed on God through devotion, so too by desire, hatred, fear, and affection, many have become freed from sin and attained the state of God. The gopis attained Shri Krishna through desire, Kansa through fear, kings like Shishupal through hatred, the Yadavs of the Vrishni clan through kinship, you [Yudhishthir] through affection, and we through devotion.

Register No. 449, page 217, writes: To become enraptured by the Lord's divine glories (vibhutis) is itself a form of devotion. Even in the present age, though the Lord is Maryada Purushottam (the Supreme Being who upholds propriety), one who becomes enraptured by him will certainly attain a good end (sadgati). Even if someone reaches the Lord through a base desire, good still comes of it. The women of Janakpur became enraptured, and many of them looked upon him with the feeling of a husband, yet may the Lord be blessed. The women of Janakpuri became enraptured, and many looked upon him with the feeling of a husband, but the Lord did not look upon them with that same feeling. In the Ram incarnation he did not wish for additional wifehood. Those women who became enraptured desired only the state of a female companion (sakhi) — they became the gopis; those who desired wifehood became his queens.

The Garga Samhita, pages 181-182, writes: After her nose and ears were cut off, Shurpanakha performed austerities to Shiva so that Ram might become her husband; Shiva therefore told her that in the Krishna incarnation she would become Krishna's beloved. Register 449, page 218, writes that Ram himself told Shurpanakha: "In this incarnation I cannot accept you; I will fulfill your wish in the next incarnation." Shurpanakha became Kubja in the Dvapar age.

The couplet in Samagam telling how Kripanath (the Merciful Lord) had to wed Shurpanakha, who had come in the form of Kubja, is as follows:

_Saath varasni dokri, sol varasna Kahan; Chandan base Jeevna, kidhi aap saman._ ||1||
(Jivandasji Maharaj says: Kubja was an old woman of sixty years, while Shri Krishna was a youth of sixteen. Yet, on the pretext of bringing sandalwood paste, he made her as beautiful as himself and sixteen years young.)

In the 107th couplet of the Naam-rupi Sakhi it says:

_Saul varasni sundari, panch varaske Shyam; Kharak dekhavat gaye Jeevna, tab pure manke kaam._ ||10||
(Jivandasji Maharaj says: the beautiful Radha was sixteen years old, and Shri Krishna was five, yet when he went out to graze the cows, he fulfilled the desires of her heart.)

_Krishnavatar kamini, Raghupati kino jog; Ved vachan kahe Jeevna, naari leeno bhog._ ||18||
(Jivandasji Maharaj says: In the Krishna incarnation, Raghupati achieved union in love with desirous women — this is what those who truly understand the words of the Vedas have declared: that the Lord enjoyed the company of women in this way.)

Everyone in the whole universe talks of "guru, guru," but among gurus there exist countless kinds and endless views. So Samagam says:

_Guru reejo vichaarke, johi bataave Ram; Sarayu toore Jeevna, je nagar Ayodhya gaam._ ||1||
(Jivandasji Maharaj says: choose your guru with understanding and thought — one who directs you to worship the King who resides in the city named Ayodhya on the banks of the river Sarayu.)

Even when we go to buy a few paisa's or a rupee's worth of tooth-twig (datan), we check it carefully before taking it. When we go to buy grain, we hold the sample in our hand. When we go to buy cloth, we check its weave and width before taking it. Do we make such a careful examination when choosing a guru? Samagam has written that everyone in the universe says "guru, guru," but there are endless views about who a guru is — why did this need to be written? Because a single idea has become fixed in the minds of everyone in the universe: that if one is to take a guru, it should be someone who is shrotriya (learned, versed in the Vedas) and brahmanishtha (established in Brahm, absorbed in meditation on Brahm, a knower of Brahm). But see how remarkable Maharaj Jivanji's own view is: he says one should take as guru whoever leads one to the darshan, bhajan, and bhakti of Ram of Ayodhya on the banks of the Sarayu. Thus, in discussing Ram of Ayodhya, a conclusion has been reached about what kind of Ram Jivanji Maharaj had in mind, so we will not go into a lengthy discussion of that here.

In Samagam it is said that there are many kinds of gurus, so one is advised to become alert and cautious before taking a guru. A cunning guru who misguides us, leading us onto the wrong path and deceiving us, is called a "ghant guru" (a hollow, sham guru). Such hypocritical gurus live in VIP-like pomp and grandeur.

_Kabir sain hamara Ramji, jaka Dashrath baap; Duniyaku dojakh diya, hamku apna jaap._ ||2||
(Das Kabirji says: Many engage in great disputes over the name of Ram. Such scholars remain absorbed in disputation alone and become unhappy — that is, they fall into hell. But for us there is only the one name of Parabrahm, which is Ram, and it is that name we chant and remember.)

The world knows Dashrath as the father of Ram, and this misleads worldly people. The Ram whom people call the son of Dashrath is, for us, a different Ram — not the Ram counted among the ten incarnations (dashavatar), but the primal (adi) Ram, the Parabrahm who has no mother or father, who takes incarnation of his own accord. That Adi Ram is our chosen deity of worship.

_Sabke sadguru Kabirji, mamat karo gat koy; Aur duniyaku Jeevna, sadguru gharki joy._ ||3||
(Jivandasji Maharaj says: Kabirji is the sadguru of all Vaishnav devotees, so no one should insist stubbornly on claiming anyone else as sadguru. But for all others caught up in the entanglements and reputation of worldly life, it is their own household wife who is their sadguru.)

_Bhav bhanjan dukh parharan, amak karan sharir; Aad jug aadi aap ho, guru charo ju Kabir._
(O Kabirji, to remove the suffering of the ocean of existence (bhavsagar) and to save the soul from the body, from the womb, and from birth and death — you alone, from before the beginning of the ages and throughout all four ages, have eternally been the guru-sadguru of all.)

_Sabka sadguru Kabirji, durmat bhanjanhar; Bahar beetar ekasa, sadguru vasne paay._
(Das Kabirji alone is the sadguru of all; he is the destroyer of our ill intellect. Being the same both outwardly and inwardly, that is, unchanging in every way, such a sadguru remains ever steadfast and free from blemish.)

_Bhakti heeno gurustyajyo, mithyavaadi vidambakah; Swashanti na janaati, patra shanti karoti kim._
(A guru without devotion is to be abandoned; he is a fraud and a mocker who spreads falsehood. One who cannot bring about his own peace — how can he bring about another's peace?)

Guru and sadguru: one's mother and father are also gurus, one's parents-in-law are also gurus, an elder in the family is also a guru, the schoolteacher is also a guru, anyone who trains one in a trade or profession is also a guru, the priest who performs religious rites is also a guru — these are all gurus, but a guru who does not free one from the bonds of worldly existence (bhava-bandhan) is not a sadguru. It is only the one who gives Name-remembrance (naam-smaran) who is the true sadguru. (At this point the printed text repeats itself, the first run of the sentence breaking off as "and that is why Kabirji is not a sadguru" — plainly a compositor's slip.) It is only the one who gives Name-remembrance who is the sadguru, and that is why we call Kabirji the sadguru Namdev-Kabir.

The various kinds of gurus mentioned above come to a person at different stages of life. Therefore the Vaishnav Jivandasji said that the soul (atma) undergoes constant dissolution (nitya-pralay), which the Gita also affirms. The soul passes through these states:
Waking, dream, deep sleep, and turiya (the transcendent fourth state) — these are the soul's states.
Birth, old age, and death — these are the soul's three sorrows.
Sattvik, rajasik, and tamasik — these are the soul's three gunas.
Adhyatmik (pertaining to the self), adhibhautik (pertaining to material beings), and adhidaivik (pertaining to the divine) — these are the soul's three afflictions (taap).
Childhood, youth, and old age — these are the soul's states of life.
But when one takes refuge in a guru, one's birth becomes fulfilled; without taking refuge in a guru, one cannot truly be called human.

In "Tattvamasi" (Thou Art That), the word "Tat" (That) — printed here in a corrupt form, "tat_ud ishwarash" — belongs to both Ishwar (God) and Jiva (the individual soul), and is therefore all-pervading and beyond perception.

In the Beejaswa Ang, in the 22nd couplet, it is written:

_Kabir ang sakaarka, baare ang niraakaar; Baare ang niranjani, aur avastha chaar._ ||22||
(Das Kabirji says: the Lord's form-with-attributes (sakar swarup) has twelve limbs, and his formless (nirakar) aspect also has twelve limbs. These twelve-times-twelve divisions belong to the attributeless Brahm (nirgun Brahm), and it has four kinds of states. The next chapter, on the Brahm within Jagat (Maya), gives the names of these twelve kinds.)

In the Panchratnamala, 3rd edition, page 662, in Kehra 6, Kabir describes the four states:

_Jagrat swapna sushupti kahiye, turiya maahi herana ho; Chaar avasthame hoi vatate, chaitan naam thaharna ho._ ||5||
(The Lord's conscious principle passes through and merges within the four states — waking, dream, deep sleep, and turiya; having passed through these four states, its name is fixed as "Chaitan," pure consciousness.)

To show that without taking refuge in a guru one cannot be called truly human, this couplet is given:

_Kabir Harki bhakti bin, raja kutta hoy; Gali gali bhusat phire, par tuk na daare koy._ ||1||
(Das Kabirji says: without devotion to the Lord, even a king must undergo the birth of a dog, wandering from street to street barking, yet no one throws him even a scrap of food.)

_Kabir Harki bhakti bin, raja bhi khar hoy; Maati laade kumbharki, ghaas na daare koy._
(Das Kabirji says: without devotion to the Lord, even a king attains the birth of a donkey; potters load clay upon him, yet no one throws him even grass to eat.)

_Kabir Harki bhakti bin, paada hoy Patel; Dashrake din maarahi, dede ghoda gail._
(Das Kabirji says: without devotion to the Lord, even a Patel (village headman) must take the birth of a male buffalo, and on the day of Dashera he is shot and killed, sent on the path of death.)

For this reason the body of the individual soul (jivatma) undergoes constant dissolution — at night dissolution occurs and by day one awakens again. But there is said to be a great difference between the sleep of a Harijan (a devotee of Hari) and the sleep of a worldly person:

_Ek suto Jeevna, Kumbhkaran nishchint; Ek nidrae Ahalya sui, gade dhari Kamalkanth._ ||1||
(Jivandasji Maharaj says: on one hand, Kumbhkaran sleeps without any care whatsoever; on the other hand, Ahalya too lies asleep, become inert like stone, yet with her heart set on attaining the Lord, the lotus-eyed one.)

The state of a Harijan's sleep was thus shown to be of true worth, whereas the waking state of a selfish person was found to carry no worth at all. The distance between a moth and the sun is as great as the distance between the waking of a base creature (sakut) and the sleep of a Harijan. This is the couplet on the waking state, showing what happiness a Harijan gives when in the waking state:

_Kabir Harijan suta jagaiye, jape Ramko naam; Teet suta na jagaiye, saakut shukar saap._
(Das Kabirji says: if a devotee is sleeping, he should be woken, so that he may remember the name of Ram; but three creatures should never be woken from sleep — the jackal, the dog(?), and the snake.)

_Kabir kalika ramjan, mata jaisa dhing; Keval gyan dradhavate, sahama mande sing._
(Das Kabirji says: the wicked people of this Kali age are as strong and unruly as a rutting bull. If one tries to instill pure knowledge in them, they become provoked against us, as if charging with lowered horns like a bull.)

_Kabir Ram rahya je khijai, kaudhi vai gal jaai; Shukar vai kar avatarai, naak baduta khaai._
(Das Kabirji says: those who become angry when we speak to them of Ram's name become lepers, rot away, and die; then, taking birth as a pig, they thrust their snout into the mud and eat filth.)

_Kabir saapku na sarahiye, paya aur sakkar paay; Taku kabahu na dheejiye, daav pade tab khaay._
(Das Kabirji says: never praise or feed a snake milk and sugar, and never trust it — whenever it gets the chance, it will bite and devour us.)

_Kabir Harijan to suta bhala, uthkar jape jaap; E teeno jaaga bura, saakut nahar saap._
(Das Kabirji says: it is good to wake a devotee even from sleep, for on waking he will remember Ram's name; but waking these three — the jackal, the tiger, and the snake — is a very bad thing.)
